cards.front: What does the Occupational Safety and Health Act (OSH Act) require?
cards.answer: Employers must provide a workplace free of recognized hazards and follow safety standards set by OSHA.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.2 · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.2 Introduction; 3.1 Topic 3: The Legal Context of HRM
points: Passed in 1970; OSHA sits in the Department of Labor
Covered in depth in Chapter 12 (Health and Safety)

cards.front: What does the Family and Medical Leave Act (1993) provide?
cards.answer: Eligible employees at 50+ employee worksites get up to 12 weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave with health coverage.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.10 · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.10 Major Federal Employment Laws (1993–2010)
points: Reasons: birth or adoption, a family member's serious health condition, your own, military exigencies
Managers can be personally liable for FMLA retaliation

cards.front: How long is FMLA military caregiver leave?
cards.answer: Up to 26 workweeks in 12 months to care for a seriously ill or injured service member who is family or next of kin.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.10 · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.10 Major Federal Employment Laws (1993–2010)
points: Added by the 2008 amendment (with the NDAA)

cards.front: What does USERRA (1994) protect?
cards.answer: Service members' jobs: no discrimination for service, and reemployment with the seniority and pay they'd have earned.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.10 · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.10 Major Federal Employment Laws (1993–2010)
points: Covers present AND future service (applicants who may be called up)
Target lost a USERRA case with $900,000 in punitive damages

cards.front: What does HIPAA (1996) require of employers?
cards.answer: Protecting the privacy and security of employees' health information under federal standards.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.10 · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.10 Major Federal Employment Laws (1993–2010)
points: HHS sets standards for electronic exchange of health data

cards.front: What does the Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act (2008) prohibit?
cards.answer: Using, or even acquiring, genetic information, including family medical history, in employment decisions.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.10 · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.10 Major Federal Employment Laws (1993–2010)
points: Train recruiters not to ask about family health
Social media can expose genetic info (a candidate posting a parent's diagnosis)
Store any genetic info in a separate confidential medical file

cards.front: What does the Affordable Care Act (2010) require of employers?
cards.answer: Employers with 50+ full-time employees must offer health insurance; smaller firms may get incentives instead.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.10 · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.10 Major Federal Employment Laws (1993–2010)
points: Under 50 full-time employees: not required to insure
Under 25 employees: tax breaks for providing coverage; SHOP marketplace

cards.front: Is any interview question illegal by itself?
cards.answer: No; what's illegal is using protected information from the answer in a decision, so risky questions invite claims.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.10 · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.10 Major Federal Employment Laws (1993–2010); 3.23 Strategic HRM Exercise: Troublesome Interview Questions
points: Discrimination requires concrete harm: not hired, passed over, harassed
Safer swaps: 'Are you authorized to work in the U.S.?' instead of 'Are you a citizen?'

cards.front: What is affirmative action?
cards.answer: Proactive efforts to eliminate discrimination and its past effects by expanding opportunity for protected classes.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.11 · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.11 Affirmative Action
points: Executive Order 11246 (1965) required federal contractors to take affirmative action
Protected classes for AA: women and minorities; also disabled and protected veterans under other laws

cards.front: What is affirmative action NOT?
cards.answer: Not quotas, not hiring or promoting unqualified people, and not firing others; goals need only good-faith effort.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.11 · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.11 Affirmative Action
points: Numerical benchmarks reflect the availability of qualified applicants
Missing a goal isn't a violation; failing to make a good-faith effort is

cards.front: Who must have a written affirmative action plan?
cards.answer: Federal contractors with contracts of $50,000+ and 50+ employees, under Executive Order 11246.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.11 · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.11 Affirmative Action
points: Plans detail recruiting, training, promotion steps, records, and internal audits
Other reasons: voluntary, court order, or a remedy for past discrimination

cards.front: What makes an affirmative action plan legally defensible?
cards.answer: It's remedial, includes nonminorities, is temporary, and is formal and written.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.11 · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.11 Affirmative Action
points: Remedial: fixes an actual imbalance
Temporary: ends when goals are met
Cases: Steelworkers v. Weber, Wygant v. Jackson Board of Education

cards.front: What is preferential treatment, and when is it allowed?
cards.answer: Giving a protected-group member an employment preference; allowed only temporarily under a court settlement.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.11 · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.11 Affirmative Action
points: A company can't decide on its own to give preferences
Better: hire for the business-related trait (e.g., ties to a community), not the protected trait

cards.front: What makes a worker an independent contractor rather than an employee?
cards.answer: The client controls only the result; if the company controls what and how the work is done, it's an employee.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.12 · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.12 Independent Contractors
points: Contractors pay their own Social Security and employment taxes
Misclassification = back taxes plus penalties (Illinois fined one firm $328,500)

cards.front: How do quid pro quo and hostile environment harassment differ?
cards.answer: Quid pro quo ties job outcomes to sexual favors; hostile environment is conduct making work intimidating or offensive.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.13 · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.13 Types of Employment Lawsuits: Sexual Harassment
points: Hostile environment victims need not be the target
Harassers can be supervisors, coworkers, clients, or customers; anyone can be a victim
Minor teasing or isolated incidents usually aren't illegal; frequent or severe conduct is

cards.front: When is an employer liable for harassment?
cards.answer: If supervisor harassment caused a tangible action; else, unless it used reasonable care and the victim didn't report.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.13 · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.13 Types of Employment Lawsuits: Sexual Harassment
points: Reasonable care = prevent and promptly correct
Remedies: back pay, reinstatement, compensatory and punitive damages, attorney fees

cards.front: What should an effective harassment policy include?
cards.answer: A clear definition and zero tolerance, how to report, how investigations work, plus annual training and audits.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.14 · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.14 Case Study: Developing a Sexual Harassment Policy
points: Extra training for supervisors on handling complaints
Keep training records to show good-faith prevention in court

cards.front: How do disparate treatment and adverse impact differ?
cards.answer: Disparate treatment is intentional, using different standards; adverse impact is a neutral rule with unequal results.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.15 · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.15 Employment Lawsuits: Disparate Treatment and Adverse Impact
points: Disparate treatment: the decision would change if the person's protected trait were different
Adverse impact: same standards, unequal consequences, intent doesn't matter

cards.front: What must a plaintiff show for a prima facie disparate treatment case?
cards.answer: Protected group member, applied and qualified, rejected anyway, and the job stayed open to similar applicants.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.15 · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.15 Employment Lawsuits: Disparate Treatment and Adverse Impact
points: From McDonnell Douglas v. Green (1973)
Then the employer must give a legitimate, nondiscriminatory reason; the plaintiff can show it's a pretext

cards.front: What defense fits each type of discrimination claim?
cards.answer: Disparate treatment: a BFOQ or legitimate nondiscriminatory reason; adverse impact: job-related business necessity.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.15 · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.15 Employment Lawsuits: Disparate Treatment and Adverse Impact
points: Job-related assessment = one that predicts performance in that job
Keep protected-trait records away from decision makers

cards.front: What is the four-fifths (80%) rule?
cards.answer: Adverse impact is indicated if a group's selection rate is below 80% of the most-selected group's rate.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.15 · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.15 Employment Lawsuits: Disparate Treatment and Adverse Impact
points: Example: 50% pass rate x 0.8 = 40% threshold; a 30% rate falls below it
A guideline, not formal law; courts also use 2-3 standard deviations

cards.front: Why is Griggs v. Duke Power Co. (1971) important?
cards.answer: It set up adverse impact: diploma and test rules that screened out Black workers without business need broke Title VII.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.15 · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.15 Employment Lawsuits: Disparate Treatment and Adverse Impact
points: Vulnerable practices: written tests, education requirements, height and weight rules, broad criminal background checks

cards.front: What did Ricci v. DeStefano (2009) decide?
cards.answer: An employer can't throw out valid test results just because they produce adverse impact.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.15 · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.15 Employment Lawsuits: Disparate Treatment and Adverse Impact
points: New Haven discarded a firefighter promotion test
Lesson: use valid, job-related assessments from the start

cards.front: What is race norming, and is it legal?
cards.answer: Adjusting scores or cutoffs by race or another protected group; the Civil Rights Act of 1991 bans it.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.15 · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.15 Employment Lawsuits: Disparate Treatment and Adverse Impact

cards.front: What is fraudulent recruitment?
cards.answer: Misrepresenting the job or company to win a recruit; even oral promises can lead to a lawsuit.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.16 · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.16 Employment Lawsuits: Fraudulent Recruitment, Negligent Hiring, and Retaliation
points: A tort claim: needs a false material fact, knowledge, intended and justified reliance, and damages
A Colorado court upheld $250,000 for hiding layoff risk
Qualify positive statements so they aren't guarantees

cards.front: What is negligent hiring?
cards.answer: Hiring someone you knew or should have known could harm others, without using reasonable care in screening.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.16 · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.16 Employment Lawsuits: Fraudulent Recruitment, Negligent Hiring, and Retaliation
points: Riskiest jobs: customer, child, or in-home contact (installers, delivery drivers)
Check references, criminal records, and employment gaps

cards.front: What is retaliation, and why does it matter?
cards.answer: Punishing someone for protected activity like complaining, filing a charge, or testifying; it's illegal and common.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.16 · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.16 Employment Lawsuits: Fraudulent Recruitment, Negligent Hiring, and Retaliation
points: Test: would it dissuade a reasonable employee? (refused references, excluded from training, undeserved bad review)
Petty slights usually don't count
Covers employees, applicants, and former employees

cards.front: What does the EEOC enforce?
cards.answer: Title VII, the ADEA, ADA, Equal Pay Act, Rehabilitation Act, and Civil Rights Act of 1991.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.17 · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.17 Enforcement Agencies
points: Created by Title VII; enforcement power added in 1972
Remedies: hiring or reinstatement, back pay (to judgment), front pay (after judgment), damages
Employers with 15+ employees must keep employment records; some file EEO-1 reports

cards.front: What does the OFCCP do?
cards.answer: A Labor Department office that enforces federal contractors' affirmative action duties (EO 11246, Section 503, VEVRAA).
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.17 · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.17 Enforcement Agencies
points: Covers contractors with 50+ employees and $50,000+ in federal business
Reviews triggered by data flags, random selection, or complaints; tries conciliation first

cards.front: Where do structural barriers to equal opportunity show up?
cards.answer: In recruiting, advancement, terms and conditions, and termination, e.g., referral-only hiring or unequal pay.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.18 · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.18 Legal Compliance Obstacles
points: Recruiting: narrow advertising, over-reliance on referrals
Advancement: unequal access to visible assignments and networks
Terms: unequal pay, inflexible policies, no accommodation
Termination: unfair downsizing standards

cards.front: What is stereotyping, and how does it block equal treatment?
cards.answer: Assuming everyone in a group shares the same traits, so people are judged by group rather than by their own merit.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.19 · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.19 Human Biases
points: Example: 'young people are lazy'
Rejecting someone as 'overqualified' is stereotyping; courts treat overqualified as qualified

cards.front: What is prejudice in the workplace?
cards.answer: Outright bigotry toward a group, which can clash with company values and lead to discrimination.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.19 · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.19 Human Biases
points: Reduce it through careful selection, training, and tracking each manager's diversity results

cards.front: What is perception of possible personal loss?
cards.answer: Fear that diversity efforts will cost you opportunities, which leads people to withhold help from diverse colleagues.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.19 · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.19 Human Biases
points: They may refer, evaluate, train, or develop others less fairly
Counter it by stressing that the focus is objectivity and EEO, not preferences

cards.front: What is ignorance as an EEO barrier?
cards.answer: Not knowing what employment law requires; it's never a legal defense, and it feeds stereotyping.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.19 · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.19 Human Biases
points: Common in small firms and with untrained managers
Mathis v. Phillips Chevrolet: untrained hiring managers were an 'extraordinary mistake'

cards.front: How can bias create barriers to equal treatment? (model answer)
cards.answer: Biased judgments replace job-related facts, so qualified people get passed over, rated unfairly, or left undeveloped.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.19 · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.19 Human Biases; 3.23 Strategic HRM Exercise: Troublesome Interview Questions
points: Model sentence: 'Stereotyping leads a manager to judge an applicant by assumptions about her group instead of her skills.'
Fixes: structured, job-related criteria; bias training; diversity scorecards for managers (Salesforce)

cards.front: What are unconscious biases?
cards.answer: Involuntary favorable or unfavorable attitudes and stereotypes that shape decisions without our awareness.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.23 · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.23 Strategic HRM Exercise: Troublesome Interview Questions
points: Tools: implicit bias tests, the Stroop effect
Counter with diverse leadership and senior advocates for diverse employees

cards.front: How do motivated blindness and rationalization differ?
cards.answer: Motivated blindness ignores inconvenient facts; rationalization excuses wrongdoing because 'everyone does it.'
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.20 · Strategic HRM
cards.note: Read more: 3.20 Barriers to Ethical HRM
points: Euphemisms like 'creative accounting' are warning signs of rationalization

cards.front: How do lowered thresholds and a lack of moral courage lead to unethical HR decisions?
cards.answer: Small lapses make bigger ones easier, and people who know what's right still don't act because of the risks.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.20 · Strategic HRM
cards.note: Read more: 3.20 Barriers to Ethical HRM
points: Other traps: fear of retaliation, overvaluing money
Moral courage can be developed

cards.front: What is algorithmic bias?
cards.answer: An AI tool trained on biased past decisions reproduces that bias, creating disparate impact risk.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.21 · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.21 Algorithmic Bias
points: Don't use protected traits or their proxies as predictors
Audit algorithms regularly; run them separately so bias can be caught and fixed

cards.front: An hourly, non-exempt warehouse worker logs 48 hours in a week but is paid straight time for all of it. Which law is the company violating?
cards.explanation: The FLSA requires overtime pay for non-exempt workers who exceed 40 hours in a week, along with minimum wage and recordkeeping.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.8 Apply · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.8 Major Federal Employment Laws (1935–1974)

cards.front: A female and a male lab technician do the same work with the same skill and responsibility, but he earns $6,000 more and no seniority or merit system explains it. What law applies, and what's the fix?
choices: Equal Pay Act; lower his pay to match hers
Title VII only; give her a one-time bonus
Equal Pay Act; raise her pay to match his
cards.explanation: The Equal Pay Act requires equal pay for substantially equal work. Employers must raise the underpaid employee's pay, never cut the other's.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.8 Apply · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.8 Major Federal Employment Laws (1935–1974)

cards.front: A manager posts that he wants 'digital natives' and rejects a well-qualified 58-year-old applicant. Which law is most directly at risk?
cards.explanation: The ADEA protects workers 40 and older. Code words like 'digital natives' can signal age bias. Title VII doesn't cover age.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.8 Apply · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.8 Major Federal Employment Laws (1935–1974)

cards.front: An employee is fired shortly after his manager learns he is gay. Under current federal law, which statute protects him?
choices: Title VII, which covers sexual orientation as sex discrimination
None; sexual orientation isn't federally protected
cards.explanation: A 2020 Supreme Court ruling held that Title VII's ban on sex discrimination covers sexual orientation and transgender status.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.8 Apply · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.8 Major Federal Employment Laws (1935–1974)

cards.front: A pregnant delivery driver's doctor limits her lifting. The company gives light duty to employees with temporary injuries but refuses her. Is it compliant?
choices: No; the Pregnancy Discrimination Act requires treating pregnancy like other temporary conditions
No, but only under OSH Act
Yes, if it pays her FMLA leave
cards.explanation: The PDA (an amendment to Title VII) requires pregnancy to be treated like other temporary conditions, as in Young v. UPS.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.9 Apply · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.9 Major Federal Employment Laws (1978–1990)

cards.front: A company's promotion test uses a different passing cutoff for each racial group to balance results. Which law does this violate?
choices: It's legal if it improves diversity
cards.explanation: Race norming, adjusting scores or cutoffs by race, color, religion, sex, or national origin, is banned by the Civil Rights Act of 1991.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.15 Apply · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.15 Employment Lawsuits: Disparate Treatment and Adverse Impact

cards.front: A company with 70 full-time employees offers no health insurance, assuming it's too small to be required. Is it compliant with the ACA?
choices: No; employers with 50+ full-time employees must offer coverage
Yes, as long as it pays COBRA
No; every employer of any size must insure
Yes; only firms with 500+ must offer coverage
cards.explanation: Under the ACA's employer mandate, firms with 50 or more full-time employees must provide insurance. Firms under 25 can get tax breaks for coverage.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.10 Apply · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.10 Major Federal Employment Laws (1993–2010)

cards.front: A supervisor tells the team that a coworker's health plan claims show a cancer diagnosis. Which law is most directly violated?
cards.explanation: HIPAA sets privacy and security standards for health information, and employers must protect employees' medical data.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.10 Apply · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.10 Major Federal Employment Laws (1993–2010)

cards.front: Inspectors find blocked fire exits and unguarded machinery at a plant. Which law sets the employer's duty here?
cards.explanation: The OSH Act requires employers to provide a workplace free of recognized hazards and to follow OSHA safety standards.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.2 Apply · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.2 Introduction; 3.1 Topic 3: The Legal Context of HRM

cards.front: An eligible employee at a 200-person company asks for 10 weeks off to care for her father after heart surgery. What does the law require?
choices: Two weeks off, then termination is allowed
Paid leave for the full 10 weeks
Unpaid, job-protected FMLA leave with health coverage continued
cards.explanation: FMLA gives eligible employees up to 12 workweeks of unpaid, job-protected leave to care for a parent with a serious health condition.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.10 Apply · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.10 Major Federal Employment Laws (1993–2010)

cards.front: A reservist returns from a nine-month deployment and is offered a lower-paying role with less seniority than before. Which law applies?
cards.explanation: USERRA requires reemployment with the seniority, status, and pay the service member would have had if continuously employed.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.10 Apply · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.10 Major Federal Employment Laws (1993–2010)

cards.front: Two weeks after a new hire starts, HR realizes no one completed her Form I-9. Which law, and what deadline was missed?
choices: IRCA; the I-9 is due within 3 days of hire
IRCA; before the first annual review
cards.explanation: IRCA requires employers to verify every new hire's identity and work authorization on Form I-9 within 3 days of hire.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.9 Apply · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.9 Major Federal Employment Laws (1978–1990)

cards.front: A deaf applicant asks for a sign language interpreter at her interview. Which law requires the employer to consider this?
cards.explanation: The ADA requires reasonable accommodation during hiring and employment unless it would cause undue hardship.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.9 Apply · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.9 Major Federal Employment Laws (1978–1990)

cards.front: An interviewer asks, 'Does heart disease run in your family?' Which law makes this risky?
cards.explanation: GINA bars acquiring or using genetic information, which includes family medical history, in employment decisions.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.10 Apply · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.10 Major Federal Employment Laws (1993–2010)

cards.front: A laid-off employee at a 300-person company wants to keep her family on the company health plan for a while. Which law gives her that option?
cards.explanation: COBRA lets workers who lose coverage continue group health benefits for a limited time at employers with 20+ employees.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.9 Apply · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.9 Major Federal Employment Laws (1978–1990)

cards.front: A company with 400 full-time workers closes a plant and gives employees two weeks' notice. Which law did it likely violate?
cards.explanation: WARN requires employers with 100+ full-time workers to give 60 days' notice of plant closings or mass layoffs.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.9 Apply · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.9 Major Federal Employment Laws (1978–1990)

cards.front: Employees who met after work to discuss forming a union are fired the next week. Which law protects them?
cards.explanation: The NLRA protects the right to organize and bargain collectively and bars employer retaliation for union activity.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.8 Apply · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.8 Major Federal Employment Laws (1935–1974)

cards.front: A federal contractor with a $200,000 contract does no outreach to protected veterans. Which law requires it to?
cards.explanation: VEVRAA requires federal contractors with contracts of $25,000+ to take affirmative action to employ and promote protected veterans.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.8 Apply · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.8 Major Federal Employment Laws (1935–1974)

cards.front: A federal contractor is asked about its progress toward a 7% utilization goal for employees with disabilities. Which law sets that goal?
cards.explanation: Section 503 of the Rehabilitation Act sets a 7% utilization goal for federal contractors. Missing it alone isn't a violation.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.8 Apply · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.8 Major Federal Employment Laws (1935–1974)

cards.front: A job application asks applicants to list all medical conditions and past surgeries. Is this compliant?
choices: Yes, for jobs with physical tasks
No; the ADA bars disability and medical questions before a job offer
cards.explanation: The ADA prohibits asking applicants about disabilities or medical history before an offer is made.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.9 Apply · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.9 Major Federal Employment Laws (1978–1990)

cards.front: A public company's CEO and CFO abruptly resign, and it faces a major employment lawsuit. What does Sarbanes-Oxley Section 409 require?
choices: Prompt public disclosure of these material changes
Disclosure only if the lawsuit is lost
cards.explanation: SOX Section 409 requires real-time disclosure of material changes such as executive departures and employment lawsuits.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.4 Apply · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.4 The Role of HRM in Risk Management

cards.front: A New York employee says she was denied promotion because she's a parent. Federal law doesn't list parental status. What's the best analysis?
choices: State law may protect her even though federal law doesn't
Title VII covers all family status
cards.explanation: States can protect additional groups. New York, for example, protects parental status, so check state law wherever you operate.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.7 Apply · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.7 Laws and Definitions

cards.front: A 62-year-old applicant says Title VII protects her from age discrimination. Is she right?
choices: No; age isn't protected by any federal law
Yes; age is a Title VII class
No; age is protected by the ADEA, not Title VII
cards.explanation: Title VII covers race, color, religion, sex, and national origin. Workers 40+ are protected by the ADEA.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.8 Apply · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.8 Major Federal Employment Laws (1935–1974)

cards.front: An HR manager repeatedly and deliberately refuses to use a transgender employee's stated name and pronouns in records and meetings. How do the EEOC and courts view this?
choices: A personal choice with no legal risk
Possible sex discrimination under Title VII
cards.explanation: Intentional, persistent refusal to use an employee's communicated name or pronouns has been treated as sex discrimination under Title VII.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.8 Apply · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.8 Major Federal Employment Laws (1935–1974)

cards.front: A nightclub hires only young women as bartenders, saying customers prefer it. Is this a valid BFOQ?
choices: No; customer preference can't justify a BFOQ
No, but only because age is involved
Yes; customer preference is a business need
cards.explanation: A BFOQ must be essential to doing the job. Customer preferences and stereotypes never qualify.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.8 Apply · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.8 Major Federal Employment Laws (1935–1974)

cards.front: A correctional facility requires same-gender officers to conduct strip searches on a gender-segregated unit. How should this be analyzed?
choices: Covered by the Equal Pay Act
A likely valid BFOQ, since the protected trait is essential to that duty
Illegal sex discrimination in every case
cards.explanation: A BFOQ applies when a protected trait is essential to the job, such as same-gender staffing for certain duties on segregated prison wards. Race and color are never BFOQs.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.8 Apply · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.8 Major Federal Employment Laws (1935–1974)

cards.front: A company hired 60 of 100 male applicants and 20 of 50 female applicants. Under the four-fifths rule, is there evidence of adverse impact?
choices: No; women's rate is 80% of men's
Yes; women's rate (40%) is about 67% of men's (60%)
cards.explanation: Selection rates: men 60%, women 40%. 40 ÷ 60 = 0.67, below 0.80, so adverse impact is indicated.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.15 Apply · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.15 Employment Lawsuits: Disparate Treatment and Adverse Impact

cards.front: On a hiring test, 50% of one group passes and 45% of another passes. Does the four-fifths rule flag adverse impact?
cards.explanation: The threshold is 0.8 × 50% = 40%. A 45% pass rate is above it, so the guideline doesn't flag adverse impact.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.15 Apply · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.15 Employment Lawsuits: Disparate Treatment and Adverse Impact

cards.front: A warehouse requires every applicant to lift 100 pounds, though the job only involves 30-pound boxes. Far fewer women qualify. Which claim fits best?
cards.explanation: A neutral rule applied to everyone that disproportionately excludes a protected group, without business necessity, is adverse impact.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.15 Apply · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.15 Employment Lawsuits: Disparate Treatment and Adverse Impact

cards.front: A recruiter secretly flags résumés with foreign-sounding names so they won't get interviews. Which type of discrimination is this?
cards.explanation: Deliberately treating applicants differently because of national origin is intentional, so it's disparate treatment.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.15 Apply · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.15 Employment Lawsuits: Disparate Treatment and Adverse Impact

cards.front: An employer is sued because its college-degree requirement screens out a protected group. What defense must it show?
choices: That the group is a minority of applicants
That it didn't intend to discriminate
That the requirement is job-related and consistent with business necessity
That competitors use the same requirement
cards.explanation: Intent doesn't matter in adverse impact cases. The only defense is that the practice is job-related and a business necessity (Griggs).
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.15 Apply · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.15 Employment Lawsuits: Disparate Treatment and Adverse Impact

cards.front: An AI résumé screener trained on ten years of a mostly male workforce starts downgrading applicants from women's colleges. What's happening, and what should HR do?
choices: Algorithmic bias; audit the tool, remove proxy variables, and monitor results
Disparate treatment by the vendor only
Use the tool but hide its output
cards.explanation: Training data that reflects past bias makes the model reproduce it, creating disparate impact risk. Audit regularly and drop proxies for protected traits.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.21 Apply · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.21 Algorithmic Bias

cards.front: Which action is a legitimate example of affirmative action?
choices: Recruiting at women's engineering societies and minority-serving colleges to widen the pool
Promoting underrepresented employees regardless of performance
Laying off current staff to make room for diverse hires
cards.explanation: Affirmative action expands the pool of qualified applicants and removes barriers. Quotas, unqualified preferences, and firing others are not affirmative action.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.11 Apply · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.11 Affirmative Action

cards.front: A company's informal affirmative action program excludes all nonminority candidates from a training program and has no end date. Is it defensible?
choices: Yes; any diversity effort is protected
No; plans should include nonminorities, be temporary, and be formal and written
No, because training can't be part of affirmative action
cards.explanation: Defensible plans are remedial, include nonminorities, are temporary, and are written. Excluding all nonminorities and having no end date make this one risky.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.11 Apply · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.11 Affirmative Action

cards.front: A federal contractor misses its hiring goal for women this year despite documented outreach. Has it violated its affirmative action obligations?
choices: No; missing a goal isn't a violation if it made a good-faith effort
Yes, unless it hires men less
No, because goals don't apply to contractors
cards.explanation: Affirmative action goals aren't quotas. Contractors must make good-faith efforts; failing to try, not missing a number, is the violation.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.11 Apply · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.11 Affirmative Action

cards.front: A software company with federal contracts is flagged for below-average hiring of women and gets a compliance review of its affirmative action plan. Which agency is reviewing it?
cards.explanation: The Labor Department's OFCCP enforces affirmative action duties for federal contractors, and data flags can trigger reviews.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.17 Apply · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.17 Enforcement Agencies

cards.front: A private employer with 200 workers receives a charge alleging it fired a worker because of her religion. Which agency handles it?
cards.explanation: The EEOC enforces Title VII and other anti-discrimination laws for most employers with 15+ employees.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.17 Apply · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.17 Enforcement Agencies

cards.front: A delivery firm calls its drivers 'independent contractors' but sets their hours, assigns routes, dictates procedures, and supplies the vans. How are they likely to be classified legally?
choices: Contractors, because the contract says so
Employees, because the company controls what and how the work is done
cards.explanation: Control is the test. Controlling both the result and the method makes workers employees, and misclassification brings back taxes and penalties.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.12 Apply · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.12 Independent Contractors

cards.front: A web designer bids a fixed fee for a project, uses her own equipment, sets her own hours, and advertises to other clients. How is she likely classified?
cards.explanation: When the client controls only the result and the worker runs her own business, she is an independent contractor.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.12 Apply · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.12 Independent Contractors

cards.front: A supervisor hints that an employee's promotion depends on whether she goes on dates with him. What type of harassment is this?
cards.explanation: Making a job benefit depend on submitting to sexual conduct is quid pro quo harassment.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.13 Apply · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.13 Types of Employment Lawsuits: Sexual Harassment

cards.front: Coworkers circulate crude sexual jokes by email. An employee who was never the target finds them offensive and humiliating. Can she have a claim?
choices: Only if a supervisor sent them
Yes; a hostile environment claim doesn't require being the target
cards.explanation: Hostile environment harassment covers conduct that makes work intimidating or offensive, even for people who aren't the direct target.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.13 Apply · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.13 Types of Employment Lawsuits: Sexual Harassment

cards.front: An employee reports harassment by a coworker. Her manager decides to 'see how it plays out.' What's the legal problem?
choices: The employer may be liable for failing to take prompt corrective action
The employee should have gone to the police
cards.explanation: Employers must exercise reasonable care to prevent and promptly correct harassment. Waiting exposes the company to liability.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.13 Apply · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.13 Types of Employment Lawsuits: Sexual Harassment

cards.front: After filing an EEOC charge, an employee is dropped from a training program, left out of team meetings, and given an undeserved poor review. What is this?
choices: A petty slight that isn't actionable
cards.explanation: Adverse actions that would dissuade a reasonable employee from protected activity are retaliation, which is illegal.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.16 Apply · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.16 Employment Lawsuits: Fraudulent Recruitment, Negligent Hiring, and Retaliation

cards.front: A home-repair company skips background checks to hire fast. A technician with a violent record assaults a customer in her home. What claim does the company face?
cards.explanation: Employers can be liable for hiring someone they knew or should have known could harm others. Skipping checks can count as constructive knowledge.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.16 Apply · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.16 Employment Lawsuits: Fraudulent Recruitment, Negligent Hiring, and Retaliation

cards.front: A recruiter assures a candidate the company is 'rock solid' while knowing layoffs are planned. The candidate relocates and is laid off a month later. What claim fits?
cards.explanation: Misrepresenting material facts to induce someone to take a job is fraudulent recruitment, even if the promise was oral.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.16 Apply · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.16 Employment Lawsuits: Fraudulent Recruitment, Negligent Hiring, and Retaliation

cards.front: Which interview question is the safest to ask?
choices: Are you legally authorized to work in the United States?
How long have you lived in this country?
cards.explanation: Asking about work authorization is job-related. Citizenship, birthplace, and residency questions risk national origin discrimination.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.23 Apply · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.23 Strategic HRM Exercise: Troublesome Interview Questions; 3.10 Major Federal Employment Laws (1993–2010)

cards.front: A retailer needs staff for some Sunday and holiday shifts. Which question should the interviewer ask?
choices: Do you attend church on Sundays?
Can you work the required schedule, including some weekends and holidays?
cards.explanation: Ask about the job's actual requirements. Questions about religious practice invite religious discrimination claims.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.23 Apply · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.23 Strategic HRM Exercise: Troublesome Interview Questions; 3.10 Major Federal Employment Laws (1993–2010)

cards.front: An interviewer wants to know if a candidate can make 7 a.m. shifts. Which question is best?
choices: Do you have kids to drop off?
How far away do you live?
Do you own or rent your home?
Can you reliably arrive by the 7 a.m. start time?
cards.explanation: Ask directly about the job requirement. Commute, housing, and family questions aren't job-related and can lead to discrimination claims.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.23 Apply · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.23 Strategic HRM Exercise: Troublesome Interview Questions; 3.10 Major Federal Employment Laws (1993–2010)

cards.front: For a logistics coordinator job, which military-related question is appropriate before hiring?
choices: What type of discharge did you receive?
Do you expect to be deployed soon?
Do you have military logistics experience relevant to this role?
Which branch are your parents from?
cards.explanation: Ask about service only when the experience is job-related. Discharge type can wait until after hire, and asking about future deployments risks USERRA claims.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.23 Apply · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.23 Strategic HRM Exercise: Troublesome Interview Questions; 3.10 Major Federal Employment Laws (1993–2010)

cards.front: A hiring manager skips every applicant under 25, saying 'young people don't stick around.' Which bias is this?
cards.explanation: Assuming all members of a group share the same traits is stereotyping. It judges people by group instead of individual evidence.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.19 Apply · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.19 Human Biases

cards.front: A senior engineer stops referring diverse candidates because he worries they'll compete with him for promotion. Which barrier is this?
cards.explanation: Fear that diversity will cost you opportunities leads people to withhold referrals, training, and fair evaluations.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.19 Apply · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.19 Human Biases

cards.front: A small-business owner rejects a pregnant applicant and later says he didn't know it was illegal. How does the law view his defense?
choices: Valid, since small firms are exempt
cards.explanation: Ignorance of employment law is a common EEO barrier, especially in small firms, but it never excuses a violation.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.19 Apply · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.19 Human Biases

cards.front: A hiring manager overlooks clear signs that his star hire is padding expense reports, because admitting it would make his hiring look bad. Which ethical trap is this?
cards.explanation: Motivated blindness is overlooking information we don't want to see when ignorance serves our interests.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.20 Apply · Strategic HRM
cards.note: Read more: 3.20 Barriers to Ethical HRM

cards.front: A manager refuses to promote anyone who drives a pickup truck. Is this unlawful?
choices: Probably not, unless it disproportionately harms a protected group
Yes, under the Equal Pay Act
No; managers can never be sued for promotions
Yes; it's unfair, so it's illegal
cards.explanation: Unfair isn't the same as unlawful. A non-job-related rule becomes illegal if it targets or disproportionately harms a protected group.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.5 Apply · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.5 The Importance of Employment Laws

cards.front: To limit hiring risk, a company outsources background checks to a specialist firm with its own insurance. Which risk strategy is this?
cards.explanation: Transferring risk to another party through outsourcing or insurance is risk sharing.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.4 Apply · Strategic HRM
cards.note: Read more: 3.4 The Role of HRM in Risk Management

cards.front: Which statement about diversity and inclusion is accurate?
choices: Inclusion means the same thing as diversity
D&I matters only for legal compliance
Hiring a diverse workforce guarantees success
Diversity is linked to customer satisfaction and innovation when inclusion lets people contribute
cards.explanation: Diversity is the mix; inclusion lets everyone contribute fully. Together they drive innovation and customer satisfaction, but diversity alone isn't enough.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.6 Apply · Strategic HRM
cards.note: Read more: 3.6 The Importance of Diversity and Inclusion to Business Performance

cards.front: A decision that isn't job-related, objective, or merit-based is what kind of discrimination?
cards.explanation: Unfair discrimination relies on anything other than objective, merit-based, job-related factors.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.5 Practice · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.5 The Importance of Employment Laws

cards.front: A manager fires several employees for wearing a rival sports team's colors to work. No protected group is disproportionately affected. What's the legal verdict?
choices: It broke the law because it's unfair
It broke the law because it targets one demographic
It didn't break the law; sports fans aren't a protected group
cards.explanation: Unfair isn't unlawful. Fans aren't a protected group, so it's legal unless it disproportionately harms one.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.5 Practice · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.5 The Importance of Employment Laws

cards.front: Discriminating against someone because of pregnancy, religion, or age is called a(n)...
cards.explanation: Violating federal, state, or local employment law is an unlawful employment practice.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.5 Practice · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.5 The Importance of Employment Laws

cards.front: Diversity helps foster creativity and what else?
cards.explanation: Diverse perspectives fuel creativity and innovation.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.6 Practice · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.6 The Importance of Diversity and Inclusion to Business Performance

cards.front: Which federal law prohibits job discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, or national origin?
choices: Title VII of the Civil Rights Act
cards.explanation: Title VII (1964) covers these five protected classes.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.8 Practice · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.8 Major Federal Employment Laws (1935–1974)

cards.front: Which law lets workers who lose their jobs keep group health benefits for a limited time?
cards.explanation: COBRA provides temporary continuation of group health coverage.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.9 Practice · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.9 Major Federal Employment Laws (1978–1990)

cards.front: Which law requires employers with 100+ employees to give 60 days' notice before a plant closing?
cards.explanation: The WARN Act requires 60 days' notice of closings and mass layoffs.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.9 Practice · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.9 Major Federal Employment Laws (1978–1990)

cards.front: How much FMLA leave can an eligible employee take to care for a spouse, child, or parent with a serious health condition?
cards.explanation: FMLA provides up to 12 workweeks in a 12-month period for this reason.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.10 Practice · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.10 Major Federal Employment Laws (1993–2010)

cards.front: How much FMLA leave is available to care for a family member who is a seriously ill or injured service member?
cards.explanation: Military caregiver leave allows up to 26 workweeks in a 12-month period.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.10 Practice · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.10 Major Federal Employment Laws (1993–2010)

cards.front: Demoting or firing an employee because of military service violates which law?
cards.explanation: USERRA protects service members from discrimination and guarantees reemployment. VEVRAA covers contractor affirmative action for veterans.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.10 Practice · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.10 Major Federal Employment Laws (1993–2010)

cards.front: Proactive efforts to eliminate discrimination and its past effects are called...
cards.explanation: Affirmative action is the effort itself; an affirmative action plan is the written document detailing it.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.11 Practice · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.11 Affirmative Action

cards.front: A group that has been underrepresented in employment is known as a ___ class.
cards.explanation: Protected classes are groups historically underrepresented in employment.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.11 Practice · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.11 Affirmative Action

cards.front: Which group is NOT covered by affirmative action requirements?
cards.explanation: Workers 40+ are protected from discrimination by the ADEA, but affirmative action doesn't cover them.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.11 Practice · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.11 Affirmative Action

cards.front: Executive Order 11246 requires federal contractors to...
cards.explanation: EO 11246 requires covered federal contractors to maintain affirmative action plans.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.11 Practice · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.11 Affirmative Action

cards.front: Employers that discriminated in the past may adopt which of these as a remedy?
cards.explanation: Affirmative action plans can be an agreed remedy for past discrimination.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.11 Practice · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.11 Affirmative Action

cards.front: Giving a member of a protected group a preference in an employment decision is called...
cards.explanation: Preferential treatment is allowed only temporarily in court-settled cases.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.11 Practice · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.11 Affirmative Action

cards.front: When sexual conduct is made a condition of employment or advancement, what type of harassment is it?
cards.explanation: Quid pro quo ('this for that') ties job decisions to submitting to sexual conduct.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.13 Practice · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.13 Types of Employment Lawsuits: Sexual Harassment

cards.front: When conduct leaves an employee feeling fearful, demeaned, or belittled, whether or not they were the target, it's...
cards.explanation: Hostile environment harassment creates an intimidating or offensive workplace.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.13 Practice · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.13 Types of Employment Lawsuits: Sexual Harassment

cards.front: Who is always responsible when a supervisor's harassment ends in a tangible employment action?
cards.explanation: Employers are always liable for supervisor harassment that results in a tangible action like firing or demotion.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.13 Practice · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.13 Types of Employment Lawsuits: Sexual Harassment

cards.front: When an employee complains of harassment, what should the employer do?
choices: Wait and see how it plays out
cards.explanation: Prompt corrective action is both legally required and the right thing to do.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.13 Practice · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.13 Types of Employment Lawsuits: Sexual Harassment

cards.front: Title VII bars treating people differently because of membership in a ___ group.
cards.explanation: Title VII prohibits disparate treatment based on protected group membership.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.15 Practice · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.15 Employment Lawsuits: Disparate Treatment and Adverse Impact

cards.front: If a decision would have changed had the person's race, religion, or sex been different, that is...
cards.explanation: That's the test for disparate treatment: intentional discrimination.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.15 Practice · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.15 Employment Lawsuits: Disparate Treatment and Adverse Impact

cards.front: Which Supreme Court case is the landmark for adverse impact?
cards.explanation: Griggs (1971) established that neutral practices with disproportionate effects need business necessity.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.15 Practice · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.15 Employment Lawsuits: Disparate Treatment and Adverse Impact

cards.front: A rule to hire only people 6 feet or taller reduces the number of women and some minorities hired. This is an example of...
cards.explanation: A neutral height rule with disproportionate effects on protected groups is adverse impact.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.15 Practice · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.15 Employment Lawsuits: Disparate Treatment and Adverse Impact

cards.front: Retaliating against an employee who complained about harassment is...
cards.explanation: Retaliation for protected activity is illegal.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.16 Practice · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.16 Employment Lawsuits: Fraudulent Recruitment, Negligent Hiring, and Retaliation

cards.front: Believing that all members of a group share the same traits or behaviors is called...
cards.explanation: Stereotyping judges individuals by assumptions about their group.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.19 Practice · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.19 Human Biases

cards.front: Which bias is often inaccurate and harmful and frequently leads to legal violations?
cards.explanation: Stereotypes are often wrong and can drive unlawful decisions.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.19 Practice · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.19 Human Biases

cards.front: Outright bigotry toward a group is called...
cards.explanation: Prejudice is open bias against a group.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.19 Practice · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.19 Human Biases

cards.front: Being unaware of what employment laws require is which EEO barrier?
cards.explanation: Ignorance of the law is a barrier, and it isn't a legal defense.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3.19 Practice · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.19 Human Biases

cards.front: Employment laws exist mainly because employers hold more ___ than employees.
cards.explanation: Employers control pay, promotion, and conditions, so laws limit that power.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3 Quiz Q1 · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.5 The Importance of Employment Laws

cards.front: Hiring the candidate with the best job-related skills, based on objective criteria, is an example of ___ discrimination.
cards.explanation: Fair discrimination uses only objective, merit-based, job-related factors.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3 Quiz Q2 · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.5 The Importance of Employment Laws

cards.front: Being mindful of differences in gender, nationality, orientation, disability, and culture is known as ___ awareness.
cards.explanation: Diversity awareness means understanding and valuing these differences.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3 Quiz Q3 · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.6 The Importance of Diversity and Inclusion to Business Performance

cards.front: Which law bars employers from retaliating against employees who try to unionize?
cards.explanation: The NLRA (1935) protects organizing and collective bargaining.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3 Quiz Q4 · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.8 Major Federal Employment Laws (1935–1974)

cards.front: Which law sets the federal minimum wage and overtime rules?
cards.explanation: The FLSA (1938) sets minimum wage, overtime, recordkeeping, and youth employment rules.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3 Quiz Q5 · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.8 Major Federal Employment Laws (1935–1974)

cards.front: Which law specifically prohibits paying men and women differently for equal work?
cards.explanation: The Equal Pay Act (1963) bars sex-based wage discrimination.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3 Quiz Q6 · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.8 Major Federal Employment Laws (1935–1974)

cards.front: What does FMLA stand for?
cards.explanation: The Family and Medical Leave Act (1993) provides job-protected leave.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3 Quiz Q7 · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.10 Major Federal Employment Laws (1993–2010)

cards.front: A recruiter browses a candidate's social media and sees a post about her mother's hereditary illness. Using that in a hiring decision would violate which law?
cards.explanation: GINA bars acquiring or using genetic information, including family medical history, in employment decisions, which is why social media screening is risky.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3 Quiz Q8 · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.10 Major Federal Employment Laws (1993–2010)

cards.front: Which law guarantees equal opportunity to people who have a disability or are perceived as having one?
cards.explanation: The ADA (1990) protects people with actual or perceived disabilities.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3 Quiz Q9 · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.9 Major Federal Employment Laws (1978–1990)

cards.front: Which set lists exactly the classes protected under Title VII?
choices: Color, pregnancy, national origin, religion, disability
Race, color, religion, national origin, sex
cards.explanation: Title VII names race, color, religion, sex, and national origin. Disability, veteran status, and marital status aren't on the list.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3 Quiz Q10 · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.8 Major Federal Employment Laws (1935–1974)

cards.front: Affirmative action aims to provide opportunity to members of a ___ class.
cards.explanation: Affirmative action expands opportunity for protected classes.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3 Quiz Q11 · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.11 Affirmative Action

cards.front: Which of these is an example of affirmative action?
cards.explanation: Affirmative action is a proactive effort, such as outreach to women and minorities. Basic compliance isn't proactive, and quotas aren't allowed.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3 Quiz Q12 · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.11 Affirmative Action

cards.front: Federal contractors maintain ___ because the law requires it.
cards.explanation: Executive Order 11246 requires covered federal contractors to have affirmative action plans.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3 Quiz Q13 · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.11 Affirmative Action; 3.17 Enforcement Agencies

cards.front: Lewd jokes, whistling, and offensive pictures at work can create what kind of environment?
cards.explanation: Such conduct can support a hostile environment harassment claim.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3 Quiz Q14 · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.13 Types of Employment Lawsuits: Sexual Harassment

cards.front: Who can be the victim of sexual harassment?
choices: Only people of the same sex as the harasser
cards.explanation: Victims and harassers can be any sex; courts look at the conduct.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3 Quiz Q15 · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.13 Types of Employment Lawsuits: Sexual Harassment

cards.front: In a harassment case without a tangible employment action, when is the employer liable?
choices: When it had a policy and training in place
When it didn't use reasonable care to prevent and promptly correct the harassment
When it counseled managers on retaliation
When it skipped an annual questionnaire
cards.explanation: Employers can avoid liability only if they took reasonable care and the employee unreasonably failed to complain.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3 Quiz Q16 · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.13 Types of Employment Lawsuits: Sexual Harassment

cards.front: Intentionally treating someone differently because of a protected characteristic is...
cards.explanation: Disparate treatment is intentional discrimination.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3 Quiz Q17 · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.15 Employment Lawsuits: Disparate Treatment and Adverse Impact

cards.front: A practice that disproportionately harms a protected group, whether or not anyone intended it, is...
cards.explanation: Adverse impact focuses on effects, not intent.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3 Quiz Q18 · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.15 Employment Lawsuits: Disparate Treatment and Adverse Impact

cards.front: Some employees fear they'll lose opportunities when the company hires for diversity. Which barrier is this?
cards.explanation: This fear can make people less willing to refer, train, or fairly evaluate diverse colleagues.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3 Quiz Q19 · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.19 Human Biases

cards.front: A hiring manager rejects a strong candidate as 'overqualified.' What bias does this often reflect?
cards.explanation: Assuming an overqualified person will be bored or leave is stereotyping. Courts treat overqualified as qualified.
cards.subtitle: Ch 3 Quiz Q20 · Legal & Regulatory
cards.note: Read more: 3.19 Human Biases
